weaknesses: The contribution is technically incremental. Loop detection, error-triggered critique, verification agents, and context compression are established ideas; the paper mainly packages them behind heuristic triggers. It does not experimentally compare against the most relevant runtime supervision, context-compression, or tool-overuse mitigation methods, so the benefit attributable to the proposed design is unclear.

The evaluation lacks statistical support. Claims such as "statistically equivalent" accuracy and "significant" variance reduction are made without confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or clearly documented independent runs. Several reported accuracy differences correspond to only one or two examples, especially on AIME and the 30-task GAIA ablation subset.

The ablation and cross-framework studies select the ten most token-intensive baseline tasks from each GAIA level. This selection strongly favors observing token reductions and invites regression-to-the-mean effects; it cannot substantiate general cross-framework efficiency or robustness claims.

Token accounting is insufficiently defined. It is unclear whether all supervisor, summarization, verification-agent, failed-call, and cached tokens are included consistently. Latency, monetary cost, tool/API calls, and supervisor invocation frequency are also omitted, making the claim that the framework is "lightweight" difficult to assess—particularly when GPT-4.1 or Gemini is used as the supervisor.

The broader comparisons do not establish a favorable accuracy-efficiency frontier. On several secondary benchmarks, SMAS remains dramatically more token-expensive than vanilla, self-consistency, or MetaAgent baselines for modest accuracy gains, while accuracy decreases on MBPP and DROP. Comparisons among separately configured agent systems may also confound framework quality, tools, budgets, and prompts.

The robustness claim is not adequately validated. Lower token-count variance can arise mechanically from compression or curtailed trajectories and is not, by itself, evidence of robustness. There are no controlled error-injection, misinformation-propagation, filter precision/recall, correction-success, or safety evaluations.

Reproducibility is weak despite including prompts. Key heuristic thresholds and rules, trace-window sizes, sampling parameters, execution budgets, model versions, sampled-example identities/seeds, pass@k protocol, and the list of ignored errors are incomplete. The claimed code link is blank.

There are internal inconsistencies and overclaims: the abstract reports 29.45% token reduction while the main results report 29.68%; GAIA is described as a validation set in the main text but as a private-answer test set in the appendix; and "universal," "MAS-agnostic," and "model-agnostic" conclusions are stronger than the limited, selectively evaluated evidence supports.

The supervisor can replace observations or append model-generated corrections, creating a new hallucination and control-failure surface. The paper provides no auditing mechanism, calibration analysis, or discussion of the safety and privacy implications of sending traces to supervisor and verification models.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing the high and unpredictable inference cost of multi-agent systems while preserving task performance.
SUPERVISORAGENT is conceptually simple and modular, combining error correction, inefficiency guidance, and observation compression through an adaptive trigger.
The empirical scope is broader than average, covering GAIA plus five math, coding, and question-answering benchmarks, several foundation models, and three agent frameworks.
The main full-GAIA comparison against Smolagent shows a potentially useful result: approximately 30% lower reported token consumption at unchanged pass@1 accuracy.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The method largely combines familiar heuristic monitoring, critic/supervisor prompting, error handling, and context compression. The formal definitions do not add substantive technical insight, and the paper does not convincingly distinguish the approach from prior runtime guard, verifier, and supervisory-agent systems.

Efficiency accounting is insufficiently specified. It is unclear exactly which input and output tokens from the supervisor, trace summarization, verification agent, and failed or repeated calls are included. Latency, monetary cost, tool/API calls, and intervention frequency are not reported. Consequently, the central claim of reducing total computational overhead is not adequately established.

The experimental evidence lacks uncertainty quantification. There are no confidence intervals, repeated-run statistics, hypothesis tests, or paired per-task analyses, despite stochastic LLM execution. The claim of 'statistically equivalent' success rates is unsupported.

The ablation and cross-framework studies use only the 10 most token-intensive baseline tasks from each GAIA level. This post-hoc selection strongly favors observing token reductions and makes the results vulnerable to selection bias and regression to the mean. With only 30 tasks, reported accuracy differences correspond to very few examples and cannot be described as significant.

The paper's broad robustness and generality claims are overstated. Robustness is mainly equated with lower raw token-count variance, which naturally decreases when the mean is reduced; no normalized dispersion, failure robustness, adversarial evaluation, or statistical test is provided. Most non-GAIA experiments use only one base model and one framework, while full-set cross-framework results are absent.

The method is not convincingly 'lightweight' or 'non-intrusive': it intercepts and mutates ActionStep observations, invokes another large model with execution traces, depends on framework-specific markers and callbacks, and may launch a fully equipped verification agent. The engineering effort and added failure surface are not evaluated.

Important baselines and controls are missing, including simple deterministic HTML cleaning, truncation or extractive compression, cheaper summarizers, fixed intervention schedules, and matched-budget supervisor/critic approaches. Moreover, on full GAIA, AWorld already reports substantially higher accuracy and lower token use than the proposed Smolagent-based system, weakening the practical competitiveness claim.

Reproducibility is poor. The advertised code link is blank, the inefficiency detector and exception exclusions are not fully specified, and important details such as sampling parameters, random seeds, subset identities, base-agent prompts, tool configurations, model/API versions, and precise token-counting rules are missing. The main text calls GAIA a validation-set experiment, while the appendix says the private test set with 164 tasks was used, creating an additional inconsistency.

There is no analysis of trigger precision, false interventions, hallucinated observation corrections, or negative cases. The single favorable case study is not sufficient, and its unexplained switch from the baseline's RC Pets hypothesis to Ruffwear raises questions about how the supervisor obtained the decisive information.

The paper does not meaningfully discuss safety or ethical risks arising from allowing an LLM supervisor to replace tool observations and present generated content as corrected or verified evidence. Overall, the idea is plausible and the preliminary savings are promising, but the evaluation and reporting do not support the paper's strongest claims at a top-tier-conference standard.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing the high and unpredictable inference cost of multi-agent systems without redesigning their underlying architectures.
SUPERVISORAGENT is conceptually simple and modular, combining targeted error correction, inefficiency guidance, and observation compression behind a lightweight trigger mechanism.

The empirical scope is broader than is typical for agent-efficiency work: six benchmarks, multiple task domains, three supervisor models, and integrations with Smolagent, AWorld, and OAgents are evaluated.

The main within-framework result is promising: on GAIA, adding the supervisor to Smolagent reduces average token use by 29.68% at pass@1 while preserving aggregate accuracy. Results on the five additional benchmarks also generally show meaningful token reductions with small accuracy changes.
Component ablations, cross-framework experiments, token-distribution analyses, prompts, and a concrete execution trace help explain the method and its observed gains.
The manuscript is well organized, visually polished, and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The experimental reporting lacks statistical rigor. The paper calls GAIA accuracy “statistically equivalent” but provides no confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, uncertainty across runs, or task-level paired analysis. Several claimed accuracy improvements or regressions correspond to only a few examples and may be noise.

The strongest GAIA evidence only establishes an improvement over Smolagent, not state-of-the-art efficiency. AWorld achieves substantially higher accuracy with far fewer tokens than supervised Smolagent in Table 1. Consequently, claims of a general Pareto improvement and a universal efficiency enhancer are stronger than the evidence supports.

Important cost-accounting details are insufficiently explicit. Although the figures appear to include supervisor overhead, the paper does not clearly define how tokens from supervisor decisions, interaction summaries, verification agents, retries, and cached prompts are aggregated. Latency, monetary cost, tool calls, and the potentially different prices of supervisor models are not reported.

The GAIA description is internally inconsistent: the main text calls the data the validation set, whereas the appendix says that the 164-task private-answer test set was used. This must be resolved because it affects verifiability and possible exposure to public answers.

The “adaptive filter” is largely a fixed conditional heuristic with a 3,000-character threshold. Critical details of the loop detector, excessive-step thresholds, defensive error exclusions, and other hyperparameters are missing, despite the claim that implementation details are provided. The advertised code link is also blank.

The ablation study uses only the 10 most token-intensive baseline tasks from each GAIA level. This small, deliberately selected subset favors demonstrating savings and cannot establish typical component effects. Full-benchmark ablations, sensitivity analyses for filter thresholds, and comparisons against simple truncation or summarization controls are needed.

Novelty is moderate: the contribution mainly integrates familiar runtime monitoring, LLM-based correction, loop detection, and context compression. The comparison with related runtime supervisory approaches, particularly AWorld's Guard and tool-overuse mitigation methods, is mostly qualitative rather than controlled.

Robustness is operationalized primarily as lower variance in token consumption. That measures cost predictability rather than resistance to misinformation or error propagation, even though proactive error correction is a central motivation. No targeted corruption, erroneous-memory, or faulty-tool experiment validates those robustness claims.

Accuracy decreases on MBPP and DROP, and GAIA Level 2 pass@1 also drops, but the paper does not characterize which information is lost during purification or define a safe operating tradeoff. An intervention-frequency and error analysis would clarify when supervision helps or harms.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reducing the substantial token cost and execution failures of LLM-based agent systems through runtime supervision.
The proposed system is modular and conceptually straightforward, combining error correction, inefficiency guidance, and observation purification with a low-cost heuristic trigger.

The empirical study covers six benchmarks, three supervisor backbones, and several agent frameworks. It also includes component ablations, threshold sensitivity, token-overhead accounting, latency measurements, failure analysis, prompts, and a concrete case study.
The principal within-framework result is promising: on GAIA, adding the supervisor to Smolagent reportedly preserves pass@1 accuracy while reducing net token consumption by 29.68%.
The manuscript is generally well organized and visually polished, with clear diagrams and readable tables.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not support several central claims with sufficient rigor. No confidence intervals, repeated-run variability, hypothesis tests, or significance analyses are reported, yet the paper calls unchanged accuracy 'statistically equivalent' and repeatedly describes small differences as improvements. This is especially problematic for AIME, where a 6.67-point change corresponds to only two of 30 questions.

The GAIA protocol is internally inconsistent. The main paper repeatedly says that the validation set was used, whereas the appendix says that the 164-task test set with private answers was used. GAIA's private test labels should not be directly available, and 164 tasks instead resembles the public validation set. This ambiguity materially harms confidence in evaluation validity and reproducibility.

The baseline evidence weakens the claimed practical impact. In Table 1, AWorld achieves both substantially higher accuracy and much lower token usage than the principal SMAS configuration. Comparisons against most alternative systems are not controlled integrations, and no strong runtime-supervision, guard, critic, or context-compression baseline is evaluated under matched models, tools, prompts, and budgets.

The claimed cross-framework generalization is based on only 30 GAIA examples selected as the most token-intensive tasks, creating selection bias toward the method's intended advantage. Moreover, the AWorld version uses mandatory semantic invocation through a modified system prompt rather than the same heuristic filter, while OAgents receives separately tuned thresholds. These materially different implementations do not establish a single MAS-agnostic mechanism.

The method is described as 'adaptive,' but its main filter consists largely of fixed thresholds, periodic calls every several steps, and exact repeated-action checks. The algorithm also omits parts of the implementation described in prose, including sub-agent completion detection and suppression of selected noncritical errors.

Efficiency is reduced to token count even though the method increases average latency by 37.27%, invokes potentially differently priced models, and does not account for tool/API calls or monetary cost. Calling the framework 'lightweight' and claiming a broad Pareto improvement are therefore overstated. Accuracy also decreases on MBPP and DROP.

The robustness claim is poorly operationalized: robustness is primarily equated with lower variance in token consumption, rather than success stability, error recovery, or resistance to misinformation. The paper provides no controlled error-injection or adversarial evaluation despite motivating the method through error propagation and factual corruption.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The advertised code link is blank, random seeds and sampling identities are missing, decoding and execution settings are incomplete, and the unusual pass@k token-accounting protocol is not explained. Token averages even vary non-monotonically across pass@1, pass@2, and pass@3, making the reported efficiency comparisons difficult to interpret.

Observation replacement and LLM-based verification can themselves hallucinate, omit decisive evidence, or corrupt downstream state. The paper acknowledges information loss but does not quantify intervention precision, false-positive rates, factual-correction accuracy, or safety regressions.

The novelty is limited relative to established supervisor, guard, critic, verification, and context-compression patterns. Positioning against the closest runtime supervisory methods is thin, and parts of the related-work discussion appear careless—for example, the appendix incorrectly describes the cited OWL agent framework as the Web Ontology Language.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: controlling the substantial token overhead and error propagation of multi-agent systems at runtime without modifying their internal architectures.
The proposed framework is intuitive and modular, combining a lightweight heuristic trigger with targeted correction, guidance, verification, and observation purification actions.

The central GAIA result is practically meaningful: the reported pass@1 configuration preserves aggregate accuracy while reducing net token consumption by 29.68%, including the supervisor's own tokens.

The evaluation is broad, covering six benchmarks, multiple task domains, several supervisor backbones, and three agent frameworks. Component ablations, threshold sensitivity, latency measurements, failure analysis, and detailed prompts further strengthen the empirical package.
The paper is generally well organized, and its figures and tables communicate the method and main efficiency results effectively.
weaknesses: The statistical support is insufficient. Claims of statistically equivalent accuracy and significantly reduced variance are made without confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or per-task paired analyses. Small accuracy changes on AIME and the 30-task cross-framework subset are especially uncertain.

The main efficiency mechanism appears to be LLM-based observation compression, but the paper lacks comparisons against simple truncation, summarization, context-compression, or budget-matched supervisor baselines. The current ablations establish internal component utility but do not show that the proposed machinery is necessary relative to simpler alternatives.

The robustness claim is overstated. Robustness is primarily evaluated through raw token-count variance, which naturally tends to decrease when the mean decreases; normalized dispersion, tail-cost statistics, repeated-run variability, and direct error-propagation measurements would be more convincing.

The model-agnostic experiment changes the supervisor model while keeping the GAIA base agents on GPT-4.1, so it provides limited evidence for broad backbone agnosticism. Likewise, cross-framework evaluation uses only the 10 most token-intensive baseline tasks per level, introducing selection bias and yielding a small sample.

There are reproducibility and protocol ambiguities: the appendix says that the private GAIA test set contains 164 evaluated tasks, whereas the reported level-wise accuracies appear consistent with the 165-example public validation set; the random subset seeds and sampling details are not reported; and the promised code link is absent in the reviewed manuscript.

The pass@k token accounting is unclear because reported average token costs do not increase monotonically with k. The paper should specify whether these are per-run averages, cost-to-success estimates, or total costs of all k attempts.

Token savings come with a substantial 37.27% average latency increase, and no monetary, energy, or tool-call cost analysis is provided. Thus, the broader claim of universal economic efficiency is stronger than the evidence supports.
